statement: The average U.S. residential electricity price was 13.15 cents per kilowatthour in 2020 and 17.23 cents in 2025.
context: EIA, a federal statistical agency, 2026-10-23 release (second Trump administration); survey of utilities (Form EIA-861M, EIA-861), revenue divided by sales, not a posted rate. Prices are nominal (not adjusted for inflation); values for 2025 are final. EIA calculates average revenue per kWh as a proxy for price.

statement: EIA said in May 2025 that retail electricity prices had increased faster than inflation since 2022 and forecast they would keep increasing through 2026, with a nominal national increase of 13% from 2022 to 2025.
anchor: Retail electricity prices have increased faster than the rate of inflation since 2022, and we expect them to continue increasing through 2026
Although we expect the nominal U.S. average electricity price to increase by 13% from 2022 to 2025
context: EIA in-brief analysis, May 2025, second Trump administration; a forecast. The measured 2022-2025 residential series (15.04 to 17.23 cents) is consistent with it; the LBNL study qualifies it by finding that real national prices were flat through 2024 and prices only began to outpace inflation in 2025.

statement: In 2025 the U.S. average residential electricity price was 17.30 cents per kilowatthour, and all-sector average prices ranged from 35.72 cents in Hawaii to 8.20 cents in North Dakota.
anchor: residential 17.30¢ per kWh
In 2025, the annual average retail electricity price for all types of electric utility customers ranged from 35.72¢ per kWh in Hawaii to 8.20¢ per kWh in North Dakota.
context: EIA explainer drawing on preliminary 2025 data (Electric Power Monthly, February 2026); the final 2025 residential average in Table 5.3 is 17.23 cents. Second Trump administration. EIA attributes Hawaii's price mainly to imported petroleum fuels.

statement: NEADA reported that since 2021 the average cost per kilowatt-hour rose 27.9 percent and the average monthly electric bill rose 29.2 percent.
anchor: Since 2021, the average cost per kilowatt-hour has risen 27.9 percent, while the average monthly electric bill has climbed 29.2 percent.
locator: Press release, "Electric Prices at a 10-Year High"
context: NEADA, the association of state LIHEAP directors, press release 2025-12-16; an advocacy group for higher LIHEAP funding using EIA data (nominal; its August 2025 report puts the inflation-adjusted per-kWh rise at about 7.5 percent). Consistent with the EIA series (13.66 cents in 2021 to 17.23 in 2025, a 26% rise).

statement: LBNL and Brattle found that U.S. average retail electricity prices rose 4.4% from January to July 2025 relative to 2024, or 1.9% when adjusted for inflation, and that nominal prices had largely tracked inflation through 2024.
anchor: Retail prices are outpacing inflation nationally: 4.4% increase in average from Jan-July 2025 relative to 2024, 1.9% when adjusted for inflation
National-average nominal retail prices have largely tracked economy-wide inflation in recent years, sharply increasing; real prices have been flat
locator: Findings slide 1; "Retail price developments in 2025" slide
context: LBNL (DOE national laboratory) with Brattle Group, October 2025, DOE-funded; a descriptive and statistical study that says it does not predict future prices. Same team as the peer-reviewed journal article (EV-CLP entry for SRC-4412); not independent of it. It qualifies the framing that prices have long outrun inflation: through 2024 real prices were flat, but 2025 broke from that.

statement: A peer-reviewed study of recent retail electricity prices found that the national rise had largely tracked inflation but state trends varied widely, and that recent utility-scale wind and solar outside renewable portfolio standard programs had no discernible impact on increased retail prices.
anchor: Although the recent national rise in retail prices has largely tracked inflation, state-level trends vary widely.
recent utility-scale wind and solar deployment that occurred outside RPS programs (but that benefited from tax incentives) had no discernible impact on increased retail prices
context: Peer-reviewed article in The Electricity Journal by the LBNL team (Wiser and colleagues), October 2025; DOE-funded research. Uses data through 2024; the authors note relationships may change as load growth accelerates. Same authors as the LBNL slide deck, so the two are not independent.

statement: EIA's November 2026 outlook puts the Henry Hub natural gas price at 2.19 dollars per million Btu in 2024 and 3.53 in 2025, and forecasts 3.37 in 2026 and 2.88 in 2027.
anchor:

context: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook, November 2026, second Trump administration. 2024 and 2025 are estimates or history, 2026 and 2027 are forecasts pending reconciliation. EIA says U.S. LNG exports and warm weather both move the path.

statement: NEADA said natural gas prices had risen nearly 50 percent over the past year as of December 2025, driven in part by rapidly expanding liquefied natural gas exports.
anchor: Natural gas prices have risen nearly 50 percent over the past year, driven in part by rapidly expanding liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports
context: NEADA press release 2025-12-16, an advocacy association of state LIHEAP directors. EIA's annual Henry Hub averages show 2.19 in 2024 and 3.53 in 2025, a larger rise than 50 percent on an annual basis; the "past year" window is not defined in the release. EIA's November 2026 outlook cuts the winter 2026-27 forecast.

statement: DOE reported in December 2024 that the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found data centers consumed about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023 and are expected to consume approximately 6.7 to 12% by 2028.
anchor: The report finds that data centers consumed about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023 and are expected to consume approximately 6.7 to 12% of total U.S. electricity by 2028.
context: DOE press release 2024-12-20 (Biden administration) on a Berkeley Lab report funded by DOE; 2023 is a bottom-up model estimate and 2028 is a scenario range that depends on GPU shipments, not a forecast of record. The lab says very few companies report actual data center electricity use.

statement: The LBNL report estimated that U.S. data centers used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of U.S. electricity, and that 2028 use would be roughly 325 to 580 TWh, or 6.7% to 12.0% of consumption, a power demand of 74 to 132 GW.
anchor: reaching 176 TWh by 2023, representing 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption.
the low and high end of roughly 325 and 580 TWh in 2028
a total power demand for data centers between 74 and 132 GW. This annual energy use also represents 6.7% to 12.0% of total U.S. electricity consumption forecasted for 2028.
context: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, December 2024 (Biden administration; DOE-funded), by the lab's data center research group; same report as the DOE release, so not independent of it. Estimates after 2023 are scenarios; the 74 to 132 GW assumes 50% average capacity utilization. Researchers outside the lab have given other estimates.

statement: The LBNL report says its bottom-up estimate relies on limited public and proprietary data, and that the lack of direct energy data in a rapidly evolving sector limits the analysis, especially for future demand scenarios.
anchor: The lack of direct energy data available in a sector with rapidly evolving technologies limits the analysis in this report, especially when trying to understand and estimate future energy demand scenarios.
context: LBNL, December 2024; the authors' own statement of uncertainty, which applies to the 2028 range. Biden administration; DOE-funded.

statement: Grid Strategies found that the five-year forecast of U.S. utility peak load growth rose from 24 GW to 166 GW over the past three years, a factor of six, and that data centers account for about 55% of forecast demand growth.
anchor: Over the past three years, the 5-year forecast of utility peak load growth has increased by more than a factor of six, from 24 GW to 166 GW.
Data centers are the largest driver of demand and energy growth, accounting for about 55% of demand growth in utility load forecasts over the next five years.
context: Grid Strategies LLC, November 2025, a consultancy that advocates transmission expansion and clean energy; aggregates utility forecasts filed with FERC, which are not measured load. The report itself judges the data center portion likely overstated.

statement: Grid Strategies judged that the data center portion of utility load forecasts is likely overstated by roughly 25 GW, because market analysts indicate data center growth is unlikely to require much more than 65 GW through 2030 against a utility forecast of about 90 GW.
anchor: The data center portion of utility load forecasts is likely overstated by roughly 25 GW, based on a review of reports published by market analysts.
data center market analysts indicate that data center growth is unlikely to require much more than 65 GW through 2030.
Data center load forecast for 2030 aggregates to about 90 GW
locator: Executive Summary and "Data Center Demand" section
context: Grid Strategies LLC, November 2025; professional judgment comparing utility forecasts to market-analyst benchmarks (TD Cowen, Cleanview), as the report states. A source that supports its own forecast total but qualifies the data center share.

statement: NERC's 2025 assessment forecast that aggregate summer peak demand would rise by over 224 GW over ten years, 69% higher than the prior year's 132 GW projection, and winter peak by over 245 GW, with new data centers accounting for most of the increase.
anchor: The 10-year aggregated winter peak demand is forecast to rise by over 245 GW
Over the 10-year period, aggregated assessment area summer peak demand is forecast to rise by over 224 GW. This is 69% higher than last year’s 10-year growth projection of 132 GW.
New data centers for artificial intelligence and the digital economy account for most of the projected increase in North American electricity demand over the next 10 years.
context: NERC, an industry-funded reliability organization overseen by FERC, assessment of 2026-2035 (published January 2026); the figures are North America-wide planning-area submissions (includes Canada) and are forecasts. Corroborated by Grid Strategies using FERC filings.

statement: NERC's 2025 assessment rated MISO as high risk from 2028, and PJM, Texas RE-ERCOT and WECC-Northwest as high risk from 2029, with PJM and ERCOT at elevated risk from 2026 through 2028.
anchor: MISO (Normal Risk 2026| Elevated Risk 2027| High Risk 2028– )
PJM (Elevated Risk 2026–2028| High Risk 2029– )
Texas RE-ERCOT (Elevated Risk 2026–2028| High Risk 2029– )
WECC-Northwest (Normal Risk 2026–2028| High Risk 2029– )
context: NERC, 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (published January 2026); the risk categories are NERC probabilistic judgments about the first five years (2026-2030), based on planned resources as of July 2025 and before any accelerated MISO projects (ERAS) are counted, which NERC says could eliminate MISO's projected shortfall.

statement: NERC found that PJM's projected anticipated reserve margin for summer 2026 had fallen from 35.7% to 29.7% since the prior assessment, and that PJM expects its summer peak demand to grow by 56 GW to 210 GW in 2035.
anchor: 2026 Summer ARM has fallen from 35.7% to 29.7%
PJM expects its summer peak demand to grow by 56 GW to a total of 210 GW in 2035
context: NERC 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (January 2026); a planning forecast using PJM's submissions. NERC notes PJM's own initiatives added some capacity after the July 2025 data submittal.

statement: NERC's winter reliability assessment released in November 2025 found aggregate peak demand up 20 GW (2.5%) since the previous winter while total resources rose by only 9.4 GW, and that all areas had adequate resources for normal peak conditions but extreme cold could cause shortfalls.
anchor: the aggregate peak demand for all NERC assessment areas has risen by 20 GW (2.5%) since the previous winter.
Total BPS resources have also increased since last winter, but by a smaller amount of 9.4 GW.
All areas are assessed as having adequate resources for normal winter peak-load conditions
context: NERC, 2025-2026 Winter Reliability Assessment, released 2025-11-18; a planning assessment, not an outcome. S&P Global reported that the demand growth was more than double NERC's projected new peak capacity additions. The 2026-2027 edition (due about now) was not found.

statement: PJM's capacity auction cleared at 28.92 dollars per megawatt-day for delivery year 2024/25 and 269.92 dollars for 2025/26, with cleared supply times clearing price of 2.2 billion and 14.7 billion dollars.
locator: Executive Summary, RPM Cleared MW table
context: PJM Interconnection (grid operator) 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction report, December 2025; official auction results. The last column is cleared supply times clearing price in billions, which PJM says is not the total cost to load, because load hedged by self-supply or bilateral contracts is not exposed to the clearing price. Two zones (BGE and Dominion) cleared higher in 2025/26.

statement: PJM's capacity auctions for the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 delivery years cleared at the price caps of 329.17 and 333.44 dollars per megawatt-day.
anchor: In the 2026/2027 BRA, the RTO cleared at the price cap of $329.17.
For the 2027/2028 BRA, all prices cleared at the cap ($333.44).
context: PJM Interconnection, December 2025; official results. The cap was negotiated with Pennsylvania's governor in 2025; a Utility Dive report quotes PJM as estimating that without it the 2027/28 price would have been nearly $530 per MW-day. A later auction (2028/29, July 2026) reportedly cleared near $325 (not read from PJM directly).

statement: PJM's December 2025 capacity auction procured capacity 6,623 megawatts short of its reliability requirement, with a reserve margin of 14.8% against a 20% target.
anchor: is short of PJM’s reliability requirement by 6,623 MW
PJM continues to hold a reserve margin of 14.8%
one-event-in-10-year reliability standard of a 20% reserve margin
context: PJM press release 2025-12-17; official results from the grid operator. PJM adds that this does not necessarily mean the system cannot serve load reliably and lists mitigating factors. First auction in which committed capacity fell below the requirement.

statement: PJM said the forecast peak load for 2027/2028 is approximately 5,250 megawatts higher than the 2026/2027 auction forecast, and that nearly 5,100 megawatts of that increase is attributable to data center demand.
anchor: The forecast peak load for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year is approximately 5,250 MW higher than the forecast used for the 2026/2027 capacity auction. Nearly 5,100 MW of that increase is attributable to data center demand.
context: PJM press release 2025-12-17; this is PJM's own load forecast (a forecast of data center load, not metered load). The grid operator has a stake in how the forecast is characterized.

statement: PJM said in July 2025 it would expect the capped auction price to translate to a year-over-year increase of 1.5-5% in some customers' bills, depending on how states and utilities pass on wholesale costs, and that prices fell in two zones.
anchor: PJM would expect the cap price to translate to a year-over-year increase of 1.5–5% in some customers’ bills, depending on how load serving entities and states pass on wholesale costs to consumers.
context: PJM, the grid operator, press release 2025-07-22; the operator's own estimate of retail bill effects and it has a stake in the framing. Utilities and state agencies reported larger summer 2025 bill increases in some PJM states (LBNL notes New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland bills rose significantly in mid-2025).

statement: PJM's independent market monitor estimated that existing and forecast data center load increased 2025/2026 capacity auction revenues by $9,332,103,858, or 174.3 percent, out of $14,687,047,358 in total revenues.
anchor: data center load by itself resulted in an increase in the 2025/2026 BRA revenues of $9,332,103,858 or 174.3 percent (Scenario 88).
total revenues in the 2025/2026 BRA were $14,687,047,358 (Scenario 0).
context: Monitoring Analytics, the independent market monitor for PJM, June 2025 (revised 2025-06-05); a scenario analysis holding all else equal, not a forecast. The monitor has long urged that new data centers bring their own generation, so it has a policy position. It concludes data center load growth is the primary reason for the tight market; PJM's own load forecast is the underlying driver. Revenue is not the same as the cost charged to retail customers.

statement: LBNL and Brattle found that over 2019 to 2024 a 10% increase in statewide load reduced average retail prices by 0.6 cents per kWh, and that states with the highest load growth generally saw real prices decline.
anchor: Based on state-level retail price changes from 2019 to 2024, statistical analysis suggests that a 10% increase in statewide load reduced overall average prices by 0.6 cents/kwh
Over the past 5 years, states with the highest load growth generally saw retail electricity prices decline in real terms
context: LBNL (DOE national laboratory) with Brattle Group, October 2025, DOE-funded. The finding is about 2019-2024, before the data center surge; the authors say residential customers benefited less and that the relationship was smaller and statistically insignificant for residential prices alone. It contests the claim that load growth itself raises household bills, but not the capacity-market effect.

statement: LBNL and Brattle cautioned that load growth was modest over the period they studied but is now accelerating, and that higher growth can increase retail prices if new supply and delivery infrastructure is constrained and costly.
anchor: National load growth was modest over the time-period of focus for this slide deck but is now accelerating, which may change future price drivers.
a higher growth future can increase retail prices if new supply and delivery infrastructure is constrained and costly—as it currently appears to be in some or many states
context: LBNL with Brattle Group, October 2025; the authors' own caveat to their finding that load growth lowered prices through 2024. Same team as EV-CLP entry for the journal article.

statement: A Harvard Law School review of 40 state utility commission proceedings on data center special contracts found regulators frequently approve them in short and conclusory orders, and the authors argue such contracts can shift data center costs to other ratepayers.
anchor: Our review of 40 state PUC proceedings about special contracts with data centers finds that regulators frequently approve special contracts in short and conclusory orders.
special contracts between utilities and data centers, approved through opaque regulatory processes, are transferring data center costs to other consumers.
context: Harvard Electricity Law Initiative (Peskoe and Martin), March 2025; a legal analysis by authors who argue for consumer protections, not a measured bill effect. Stance: skeptical of utility claims that special contracts shield other customers; it identifies risks and does not quantify how much household bills have risen. Not peer reviewed.

statement: NEADA estimated that one in six U.S. households was behind on energy bills, owing utilities a combined $23 billion, as of December 2025.
anchor: NEADA estimates that one in six U.S. households is already behind on energy bills, owing utilities a combined $23 billion.
locator: Press release, "Millions at Risk of Energy Insecurity"
context: NEADA press release 2025-12-16, an advocacy association of state LIHEAP directors that wants LIHEAP raised to $6.1 billion. An estimate from NEADA's own analysis; its August 2025 report gave $21 billion for June 2025 and $17.5 billion for January 2023. No official national count of utility arrears exists.

statement: NEADA estimated that utility shutoffs reached 3.0 million in 2023 and 3.5 million in 2024 and could reach 4.0 million in 2025.
anchor: Shut offs are climbing too: 3.0 million in 2023, 3.5 million in 2024, and potentially 4.0 million in 2025 according to NEADA’s analysis of utility-reported shutoff data.
context: NEADA press release 2025-10-21, an advocacy association of state LIHEAP directors; its estimate from utility-reported data that cover only part of the country. The 2025 figure is a projection. Most customers disconnected have service restored within days (per NEADA to CBS).

statement: CBS News reported that no official national count of utility cutoffs exists, and that NEADA estimates 3.5 million American households had their power cut off at some point in 2024.
anchor: While no official national count of utility cutoffs exists, NEADA estimates that 3.5 million American households had their power cut off at some point in 2024 based on public data reported by utility companies.
context: CBS News report (2025) quoting NEADA, an advocacy association of state LIHEAP directors. Included for the statement that no official count exists; the 3.5 million is NEADA's estimate, not government data.

statement: A peer-reviewed analysis of Census Household Pulse Survey data from December 2022 to September 2024 found that 22.4% of U.S. adults reported being unable to pay an energy bill, 22.0% kept the home at an unsafe temperature, and 33.6% forwent expenses such as food or medicine to pay an energy bill in the past year.
anchor: This nationally representative study relied on repeated cross-sectional survey data from the US Census Bureau’s online Household Pulse Survey administered between December 9, 2022, and September 16, 2024.

One-fifth of the population reported they were unable to pay an energy bill (42 029 443 [22.4%]). Similarly, 41 126 954 respondents (22.0%) kept home temperatures at unsafe or unhealthy levels due to cost concerns. A higher prevalence of households—63 009 461 (33.6%)—reported forgoing expenses
context: JAMA Network Open, 2025 (Graff and Aung), peer-reviewed; uses U.S. Census Bureau Household Pulse Survey, an online survey with low response rates (4.7% in the final cycle). Shares are of adults, pooled over 2022-2024, with the past 12 months as the reference period. The Household Pulse Survey ended in 2024; a Census successor was not checked.

statement: NEADA reported that the Census Household Pulse Survey showed 23.4% of households could not pay their energy bill for at least one month in the last year, up from 22.0% in 2023, and 37.4% of households earning under $50k.
anchor: The Census Bureau’s Pulse Survey reported 23.4% of households could not pay their energy bill for at least one month in the last year, an increase from 22.0% in 2023.
for low income households, those earning less than $50k, during this same period, the percent of households that could not pay their utility increased from 35.5% to 37.4%.
context: NEADA report August 2025 quoting Census Household Pulse Survey tabulations (second source for the same survey as the JAMA study, so it is a restatement of Census data through an advocacy group). The survey cycle is the one ending 2024-09; its low response rate is a limit.

statement: ACEEE found U.S. households spend a median of 3.1% of income on home energy bills, and low-income households 8.1% compared with 2.3% for non-low-income households, using 2017 data.
anchor: We find that the median national energy burden is 3.1%, and that the median low income (≤ 200% FPL) household energy burden is 3.5 times higher than the non-low-income household energy burden (8.1% versus 2.3%).
The study, based on the most recent available federal data, reflects conditions in 2017
context: American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy, September 2020 (a research nonprofit that advocates efficiency); modeled burden from the Census American Housing Survey for 2017, before the 2021-2025 price rise. The 2026 ACEEE update could not be read directly; its summary slide gives a similar median of 3.1% and low-income 8.1%. Low income means under 200% of the federal poverty level.

statement: DOE's LEAD Tool shows the national average energy burden for low-income households is 6%, three times higher than for non-low-income households at 2%, and 42% of U.S. households, about 51 million, are identified as low-income.
anchor: the national average energy burden for low-income households is 6% (i.e. an AMI of 0-80% as defined by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development ), which is three times higher than that for non-low-income households, which is estimated at 2%.
42% of U.S. households, or about 51 million, are identified as low-income.
locator: Energy Burden definition and national summary
context: U.S. Department of Energy LEAD Tool page, second Trump administration (page current in 2026); model estimates built from Census ACS 5-year 2018-2022 and EIA utility data, so burdens reflect pre-2023 prices. "Low-income" here is up to 80% of area median income, a wider group than ACEEE's 200% of poverty, so the 6% and ACEEE's 8.1% are not directly comparable.

statement: Roll Call reported in April 2026 that the second Trump administration's fiscal 2027 budget proposed zeroing out the $4 billion for LIHEAP, the sixth Trump budget to seek its elimination, and that Congress funded the program at $4.13 billion in fiscal 2026, a $20 million increase.
anchor: The administration’s fiscal 2027 budget request for the HHS proposed zeroing out the $4 billion funding for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program received in the current fiscal year.

This is the sixth Trump budget that has sought to eliminate funding for LIHEAP. Congress has rejected these requests, including the current Republican majority, which funded the program at $4.13 billion, a $20 million increase, for fiscal 2026.
context: Roll Call news report 2026-04-24. The $4.13 billion figure differs from Utility Dive's "about $4.05 billion" for the regular block grant (the $4.13 billion may include $100 million of infrastructure law money); the appropriation text and the HHS release table were not read. The request is the administration's position (second Trump administration, which argues LIHEAP is a pass-through to utilities); Congress rejected it.

statement: Utility Dive reported that LIHEAP received about $4.05 billion in the appropriations package signed in February 2026, and that the administration laid off approximately two dozen staffers running LIHEAP the previous April and then requested no funding for the program.
anchor: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, received about $4.05 billion as part of an appropriations package that will fund most government agencies through September.
In April of last year, the Trump administration laid off approximately two dozen staffers running LIHEAP as part of a broader restructuring of HHS.
context: Utility Dive trade news report 2026-02-04. The layoffs were by the second Trump administration (HHS restructuring); a House letter cites 25 staff of the Office of Community Services (not read directly). Funding figure conflicts with Roll Call's $4.13 billion; the likely reconciliation is regular funds plus infrastructure-law money.

statement: University researchers wrote in 2025 that LIHEAP funding has never been high enough to meet need, providing assistance to just 16% of eligible households in 2020, and that the 2026 budget proposal zeroed out LIHEAP while the entire staff of the LIHEAP office was laid off on April 1, 2025.
anchor: the administration’s 2026 budget proposal zeros out funding for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP
on April 1, 2025, the administration laid off the entire staff of the LIHEAP office.
In 2020, LIHEAP provided assistance to just 16% of eligible households.
context: The Conversation commentary, 2025-05-13, by university researchers who study energy insecurity; advocacy-leaning commentary, not a data source. It describes the second Trump administration's actions. The 16% figure is from HHS data via the authors.

statement: The National Low Income Housing Coalition reported, citing HHS, that an estimated 5.9 million families, 17% of estimated eligible households, received LIHEAP assistance in fiscal year 2024 through the regular program.
anchor: an estimated 5.9 million families (17% of estimated eligible households) received Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) assistance in fiscal year (FY) 2024 through the regular LIHEAP program
context: NLIHC Advocates' Guide 2026 chapter by a National Consumer Law Center attorney, citing the HHS LIHEAP Data Warehouse (original not read). Housing-advocacy source; the underlying data are HHS administrative counts. Eligibility is up to 150% of poverty or 60% of state median income.

statement: CRS reported that the percentage of federally eligible households receiving LIHEAP heating or winter crisis assistance hovered between 14% and 16% before FY2009, rose to 21% and 22% in FY2009 and FY2010 when appropriations reached $5.1 billion, and settled again at 16% in FY2013 and FY2014.
anchor: the percentage of federally eligible households receiving assistance hovered between 14% and 16%, settling at 16% for FY2006 through FY2008. However, in FY2009 and FY2010, with increased funding for LIHEAP, 21% and 22% of those households federally eligible under the LIHEAP statute were served, respectively.
the percentage of eligible households served settled again at 16% in FY2013 and FY2014.
Appropriations reached $5.1 billion for LIHEAP in both FY2009 and FY2010
context: Congressional Research Service (nonpartisan), report dated about 2018; heating and winter crisis assistance only, data through FY2014. Shows reach rises and falls with appropriations. Current CRS report with FY2023-24 figures was not found.

statement: EIA reported that U.S. electricity customers experienced an average of 11 hours of electricity interruptions in 2024, nearly twice the annual average of the decade before, and that major events such as Hurricanes Beryl, Helene and Milton accounted for 80% of the hours without electricity.
anchor: U.S. electricity customers experienced an average of 11 hours of electricity interruptions in 2024, or nearly twice as many as the annual average experienced in the decade before
Major events such as Hurricanes Beryl, Helene, and Milton accounted for 80% of the hours without electricity in 2024.
context: EIA Today in Energy 2025-12-01, Electric Power Annual 2024 (second Trump administration); utility-reported SAIDI data on a voluntary-reporting basis, with varying coverage by state.

statement: EIA reported that interruptions attributed to major events averaged nearly nine hours in 2024 versus nearly four hours per year in 2014 through 2023, while interruptions not triggered by major events routinely average about two hours per year.
anchor: Interruptions attributed to major events averaged nearly nine hours in 2024, compared with an average of nearly four hours per year in 2014 through 2023. Service interruptions that aren’t triggered by major events routinely average about two hours per year.
context: EIA Today in Energy 2025-12-01, second Trump administration; utility-reported SAIDI. Whether a day counts as a "major event" is set by each utility's IEEE 1366 threshold, so the split depends on utility reporting.

statement: The Texas Department of State Health Services' final report counted 246 deaths from the February 2021 Winter Storm Uri, close to two-thirds of them from hypothermia.
anchor: Texas has added 36 more deaths to the official death toll from the February snow and ice storm, bringing the total to 246 in what was one of the worst natural disasters in the state's history.
Close to two-thirds of the deaths were due to hypothermia.
context: Texas DSHS Disaster Mortality Surveillance Unit final report (2021-12-31), as reported by The Texas Tribune; not all deaths are from the power outage specifically (also carbon monoxide, crashes and others). The DSHS report was not read directly. The count is official but widely seen as an undercount (see the excess-mortality entry).

statement: An excess-mortality estimate cited by the Austin Monitor put the number of Texas deaths that statistically should not have happened during Winter Storm Uri at 814, more than three times the official count of 246.
anchor: Manjula was one of 246 people who officially died as a result of the storm
Karlinsky estimates 814 deaths statistically should not have happened when they did in Texas. That’s more than three times higher than the official state count.
context: KUT/Austin Monitor 2022-08-05 reporting an estimate by researcher Ariel Karlinsky; a statistical estimate and not a death certificate count, as the Texas DSHS points out. Excess deaths include those with other causes during the same period.

statement: FERC and NERC reported that ERCOT ordered 20,000 megawatts of rolling blackouts in February 2021, the largest manually controlled load shedding event in U.S. history, and that more than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for as long as four days.

more than 1,700 power generating units saw 3,565 unplanned outages, derates (a loss of generating capacity) or failures to start.

remain about 20% below 2005 levels, the benchmark for US commitments under the Paris Agreement.
